title: Lights out at 2:06
note: Fictional unit and patients. The charge nurse leads; your unit’s emergency plan and your training set what you may do.
intro: You are the dialysis technician on the afternoon shift. At 14:06 the power fails. The generator does not start. Machines are alarming, some on battery, some dark. Ten patients are connected. The charge nurse, Ms. Remy Santos, is leading.

choices.text: Go to the patients, report which machines are on battery or dark, bring lights and cranks, start nothing new.
choices.feedback: Go to the patients, not the switchboard. Your first report is short: what happened, where, and how many are connected. The leader needs to see the whole floor at once.

choices.text: Run to the generator room to try to start it, since getting power back is the fastest way to help every patient.
choices.feedback: The patients come first, and the leader needs your report from the floor. The generator is someone else’s assigned job.
choices.then: Ms. Santos calls you back to the floor. You report the machine status.

choices.text: Switch the dark machines off and on to restart them.
choices.feedback: Restarting a machine with a patient connected can disturb the circuit and its safety systems. Do not switch machines off and on; tell the leader.
choices.then: You stop and report the machine status instead.

vitals.st8: Manual blood return by nurse; foam near venous chamber

n2.scene: Ms. Santos decides to end treatments. At Station 8, a nurse is returning blood by hand with the crank, in the dark. Holding the flashlight, you see foam and air moving up the venous line toward the patient. The air detector may not be protecting him during manual return.

choices.text: Say at once: “Stop: air in the venous line!”
choices.feedback: Never return blood through a line that contains air. During manual return the safety clamp may not work, so the person watching the line is the protection. Speaking up immediately is your job.
choices.then: The nurse stops cranking and clamps the line. The air did not reach the patient.

vitals.st8: Stopped and clamped; blood not returned

choices.text: Say nothing; the nurse is in charge of the circuit.
choices.feedback: The nurse handles the circuit, but you can see what she cannot. Air entering a patient can kill. Speak up.
choices.then: The nurse notices the foam a moment later and stops. A small amount may have entered.

choices.text: Wait until she finishes the return so you don’t distract her mid-task, then tell her what you saw.
choices.feedback: By then the air is in the patient. Interrupt at once.
choices.then: You speak up a moment later; she stops and clamps.

vitals.st8: Stopped and clamped; blood not returned

n3.scene: The patient at Station 8, Mr. Nestor Ramos, starts coughing and says his chest feels tight.

choices.text: Call for help, bring the cart and oxygen, and tell the nurse exactly what you saw.
choices.feedback: Sudden cough and chest tightness after air was seen in the line can mean air embolism. The nurse and physician lead; your report of what you saw is part of the diagnosis.

vitals.st8: Oxygen on; nurse and physician leading

choices.text: Reassure him that it is the stress of the brownout, help him sit up to breathe, and keep watching him closely.
choices.feedback: Never reassure away a symptom that follows air in the line. Call for help.
choices.then: He gets worse. You call for help and bring the cart.

vitals.st8: Oxygen on; nurse and physician leading

choices.text: Run to find the physician yourself.
choices.feedback: Use the emergency call so help comes to you, and bring the cart; the leader decides who goes where.
choices.then: The charge nurse activates the call; you bring the cart.

vitals.st8: Oxygen on; nurse and physician leading

choices.text: One clock, each event with its time, words as spoken; ask if you miss a dose.
choices.feedback: The recorder writes what is said aloud, with the time. No opinions, no tidying, nothing filled in later from memory.

choices.text: Watch everything closely so nothing is missed, then write the full record afterward when the code is over.
choices.feedback: Memory after an emergency is unreliable. Write it as it happens.

choices.text: Use your phone clock and the wall clock, whichever is closer.
choices.feedback: One clock for the whole event, so the times line up.

vitals.water: RO and loop not yet checked

n5.scene: Power returns at 14:48. A nurse says, “Good, let’s reconnect the patients who didn’t finish.”

choices.text: Ask the charge nurse to hold restarts until the water technician checks the system.
choices.feedback: When power returns, do not assume the machines and the water are ready. Your account is facts: “Station 8 foam in venous line at 14:15,” not “the crank was faulty.”

choices.text: Agree and start setting up the machines.
choices.feedback: A water system that lost power may have pressure, loop, or disinfection problems. Treating on unchecked water risks every patient.
choices.then: The charge nurse holds the restart until the water technician checks the system.

choices.text: Run each machine’s self-test and restart the patients on the machines that pass, starting with those who have the most time left.
choices.feedback: Self-tests check the machines, not the water system. The water technician checks and releases the water first.

end.title: The debrief
end.text: Mr. Ramos was assessed and recovered. At the debrief, the team found that the generator’s automatic start had been switched to manual after maintenance and never switched back, and that one hand crank was missing. Each fix has a named owner and a date. Your record, with one clock and spoken words, made the review straightforward.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Power failure: go to the patients, report machine status, bring lights and cranks, start nothing new.
  • During manual return, you may be the air detector. Say “stop” at once.
  • Symptoms after air in the line: call for help, bring the cart, report what you saw.
  • Recorder: one clock, words as spoken, nothing filled in later.
  • Power back does not mean water ready.

See First response and team roles, Jobs at a code and The first five minutes.
